      {"@context":"http://schema.org","@graph":[{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/healthnewzealand"},"datePublished":"2026-07-13T00:12:13.439Z","headline":"Rachel Haggerty discusses the new FIT test pathway ","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_rachel-haggerty-discusses-the-new-fit-test-activity-7482225337377050624-TI1B","text":"A new approach to bowel symptom assessment is now live across New Zealand 🎉 

From 1 July, we have implemented the FIT for Symptomatic pathway, using the Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) to help assess and prioritise people referred for specialist assessment with bowel symptoms. The programme aims to fast-track bowel cancer care and reduce colonoscopy waitlists by up to 30 per cent.

FIT is a simple at-home test that can help clinicians assess a patient's risk of serious bowel conditions, including bowel cancer, and determine who needs more urgent investigation. This means people at higher risk can be seen sooner, while others can avoid unnecessary invasive procedures and gain reassurance more quickly.

An important point: this pathway is based on symptoms, not age. If someone has bowel symptoms and is referred by their GP, FIT may be recommended regardless of how old they are. This is different to the National Bowel Screening Programme, which is for eligible people (aged 58-74) without symptoms. The National Bowel Screening Programme age of fist eligibility will be lowered down to age 56, from September this year. 

This is another step towards providing the right care, at the right time, for the right people.

Learn more: http://spr.ly/6043BErZ7P","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_rachel-haggerty-discusses-the-new-fit-test-activity-7482225337377050624-TI1B"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/healthnewzealand"},"datePublished":"2026-07-07T20:45:00.783Z","headline":"The Sterile Journey","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_the-sterile-journey-activity-7480361251760439296-Nu3Z","text":"Behind the scenes of hospital sterilisation 👀🐛
","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_the-sterile-journey-activity-7480361251760439296-Nu3Z"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/healthnewzealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-30T02:40:18.303Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_world-social-media-day-every-year-health-activity-7477551560953102337-e74p","text":"🌏 World Social Media Day

Every year, Health New Zealand's social media team answers 50,000-80,000 questions, direct messages and comments.

We help people find trusted health information, understand health updates, and connect with the services and support they need. We're a front door to the health system.

Alongside those conversations, we also see abuse between the people in the comment section, and towards our team moderating. The comments in this image are real examples. 

Social media can be a powerful force for connection, learning and support. Every comment, post and share helps shape the kind of online environment we're creating together.

Before you post, comment or share on any social media content, take a moment:
💭 Is it accurate?
💭 Is it helpful?
💭 Would I say this to someone face-to-face?

It's okay to disagree with each other. But remember words have power. There's a real person on the other side of the screen. (And the occasional pesky bot.)

If online experiences are affecting your wellbeing, check the first comment for support and resources.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_world-social-media-day-every-year-health-activity-7477551560953102337-e74p"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/healthnewzealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-23T19:47:55.032Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_more-patients-have-accessed-care-sooner-over-activity-7475273452959117312-gitR","text":"More patients have accessed care sooner over the last year. 

This quarter, we have met or exceeded four of the five mental health and addiction (MH&A) targets.

We remain focused on providing timely access to mental health and addiction care and support for all New Zealanders.

It’s positive to see these results improving but we know there’s more work to be done.

Find more information at: https://lnkd.in/ebaDYWcN","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_more-patients-have-accessed-care-sooner-over-activity-7475273452959117312-gitR"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/healthnewzealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-23T04:47:02.077Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_i-came-to-new-zealand-from-saudi-arabia-activity-7475046738429562880-0Z5K","text":"“I came to New Zealand from Saudi Arabia to study medicine on a scholarship, and I’ve built both my professional and personal life here. 

Becoming a doctor was somewhat serendipitous. I didn’t grow up with a lifelong plan to pursue medicine, but when the opportunity arose, I took it. Over time, I discovered how meaningful the profession could be. 

What kept me in medicine was seeing the difference compassionate, evidence-based care can make. 

Medicine combines science, problem-solving and human connection in a way that few careers do. The more patients I met, the more I felt this was where I was meant to be. 

A good day is one where patients receive excellent care, the team works well together, and everyone feels supported. That sense of shared purpose is something I value deeply in medicine. 

It is especially rewarding when I can make a meaningful difference for a patient or family- whether that means helping someone recover from serious illness or taking the time to listen and explain what is happening. 

One of the harder parts is carrying the emotional weight of the job. We meet people on difficult days, and those experiences can stay with you. During intense shifts, I focus on the patient in front of me, take things one step at a time and rely on the team around me. 

Outside work, my family and Muslim faith keep me grounded. Spending time with my daughter helps me recharge and reminds me of what matters most. 

I’m proud of the journey -  coming to New Zealand as a student, completing a PhD, and now training in two specialties. 

I want to be a doctor who combines scientific excellence with genuine compassion. Patients are more than diagnoses and test results. I want them and their families to feel listened to, respected and cared for as people. 

My advice to aspiring doctors is to stay curious, stay humble and never lose sight of the human side of healthcare. None of us becomes a great doctor alone, we learn from our patients, colleagues and mentors every day.” 

- Dr Yassar Alamri, a resident doctor based in Christchurch, undertaking dual training in General Medicine and Intensive Care Medicine. 
","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_i-came-to-new-zealand-from-saudi-arabia-activity-7475046738429562880-0Z5K"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/healthnewzealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-23T03:05:50.704Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_the-latest-results-for-health-targets-jan-activity-7475021273383763968-___F","text":"The latest results for health targets (Jan – March 2026) show improvements compared to the same time last year, with more patients accessing care sooner: 

• Shorter waits for elective treatment – 64.9% of patients were seen within four months, up from 57.3% last year.  

• Shorter stays in emergency departments – 74.4% of patients were admitted, discharged or transferred within six hours, up from 74.2% last year.  

• Shorter waits for first specialist assessment – 61.2% of patients had an assessment within four months, up from 58.2% last year.  

• Faster cancer treatment – 86.2% of patients received cancer management within 31 days of the decision to treat, up from 84.6% last year.  

• Improved childhood immunisation – 83.5% of children fully immunised at 24 months, up from 79.3% last year.  

These results are encouraging and show that we’re on the right track. 

Find more information, including the milestones we’re aiming for this year, at: http://spr.ly/6188B6wF6G ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_the-latest-results-for-health-targets-jan-activity-7475021273383763968-___F"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/healthnewzealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-23T02:07:54.026Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_for-me-medicine-is-deeply-connected-to-activity-7475006691068178432-OUVP","text":""For me, medicine is deeply connected to family, service and the people who came before me. I’m named after my grandmother in Tonga, who was a district nurse. Our family home was almost like a second hospital; she delivered babies and cared for people throughout her community.

From a young age, my family told me I could stand on her shoulders and take that work one step further. I’ve carried that in my heart ever since.

As a resident doctor, I often describe us as the feet of the medical team. Our senior doctors help set the direction, and we’re there day to day - monitoring patients, carrying plans forward and connecting the wider team.

A good day for me is seeing someone progress. You might first meet a patient seriously unwell and connected to oxygen, then see them walking the corridors a few days later. Being part of that change is amazing.

When work becomes intense, I try to reframe where I am. I remind myself that being a doctor is a privilege, but also that my profession is not all that defines me.

I’m the eldest Tongan daughter. I have responsibilities to my family, church and community, and those parts of my life keep me grounded.

As a Tongan doctor, I know my presence adds to the fabric of healthcare - particularly when a patient sees someone who understands where they come from.

To anyone considering medicine: it's harder than you expect, and it takes support from the people who love you. But the work is needed, you are needed, and it's worthwhile.”

- Dr Emeline Mafi, a resident doctor at Middlemore Hospital.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_for-me-medicine-is-deeply-connected-to-activity-7475006691068178432-OUVP"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/healthnewzealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-18T23:36:07.799Z","headline":"Tiff takes us on a tour of a rescue helicopter","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_tiff-takes-us-on-a-tour-of-a-rescue-helicopter-activity-7473518945250209792-hprF","text":"Air ambulance crews love showing people around. 

They just prefer it’s not during an emergency 🚁

Take a look inside an aeromedical helicopter, with Tiff an Air Crew Officer from Taranaki.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_tiff-takes-us-on-a-tour-of-a-rescue-helicopter-activity-7473518945250209792-hprF"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/healthnewzealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-17T20:45:01.308Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_when-i-was-growing-up-my-family-used-to-activity-7473113496604512257-AVTV","text":"“When I was growing up, my family used to ask what I wanted to be, and I’d say Mother Teresa. Now I’m in public health, my Mum laughs about it. She says, ‘you used to always say that, and now you’re finally on the right path, helping people’.

I originally trained to be a dentist in India but, to be honest, I’d always dreamed of becoming a doctor. After working in dentistry for six months, I moved to New Zealand and started looking for different opportunities.

That led me to BreastScreen Aotearoa. My job is to encourage wāhine to participate in breast screening and help make the process easier to access and understand.

I work closely with community organisations. I’m a big believer in going to where people are, rather than expecting them to come to us, so you’ll often find me at marae, churches, temples, and local events. If a community needs us, we’ll do our best to be there.

Some of the wāhine I speak with feel nervous about breast screening or have barriers to attending. I listen and help people feel informed and supported enough to make the decision that’s right for them. We work hard to make our services culturally safe and accessible, including offering transport and translation support where needed.

If someone isn’t ready today, that’s okay. My hope is that when they are, they’ll know we’re here for them. 

I often share my own story. Last year I found a lump in my breast and was sent for a mammogram and ultrasound. I remember thinking, ‘oh my god, this is scary’.  I spent weeks worrying and imagining the worst. Thankfully, it turned out to be a non-cancerous cyst. 

The experience gave me a much deeper understanding of the fear and uncertainty many women feel and reminded me how important early detection can be. 

I tell wāhine I was lucky. Your health matters not just for you, but for the people who love and rely on you. A breast screen takes about 20 minutes, with people there who genuinely care. 

I go home feeling grateful for the work that I do. If I’ve helped one woman feel confident enough to take the next step, then it’s been a good day. 

As my Mum likes to remind me, I’ve found the path I was always meant to be on”. 

- Ritu, Health Promotion Recruitment and Retention Advisor
","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_when-i-was-growing-up-my-family-used-to-activity-7473113496604512257-AVTV"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/healthnewzealand"},"datePublished":"2026-06-08T22:00:02.591Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_behind-every-confident-clinician-is-years-activity-7469870885563318272-Ojx-","text":"Behind every confident clinician is years of training and experience.

Our Simulation Team at Wellington Regional Hospital design and deliver immersive training that helps teams from all over New Zealand prepare for high-pressure situations before they happen. Using lifelike scenarios, they bring together nurses, doctors and allied health staff to build skills, teamwork and safe decision-making.

The team looks after a specialist simulation centre and its facilities include:

✅ Specialist simulation rooms - recovery, ED and theatre
✅ Presentation and debriefing rooms
✅ Air ambulance simulator (it really 'flies', including with turbulence!)
✅ Skill-based training rooms.
✅ The centre has a range of high-fidelity simulators, part-task trainers and manikins (medical mannequins that can imitate real people including the ability to sweat, bleed, cry and more). 

These smart, capable trainers and their colleagues, behind the scenes, are playing a vital role in helping make care safer for patients across the country.  

These facilities would not be possible without the Wellington Hospitals Foundation and its incredibly generous donors, who have played a critical role in helping them come to fruition.

Health New Zealand | Capital, Coast and Hutt Valley","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/healthnewzealand_behind-every-confident-clinician-is-years-activity-7469870885563318272-Ojx-"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"Organization","name":"Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/healthnewzealand","address":{"type":"PostalAddress","addressLocality":"Wellington","addressCountry":"NZ"},"description":"We oversee New Zealand’s health services, from hospitals and specialists to community care like GPs.     <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        attributed-text-segment-list__content-truncated" dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">A new approach to bowel symptom assessment is now live across New Zealand 🎉 

From 1 July, we have implemented the FIT for Symptomatic pathway, using the Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) to help assess and prioritise people referred for specialist assessment with bowel symptoms. The programme aims to fast-track bowel cancer care and reduce colonoscopy waitlists by up to 30 per cent.

FIT is a simple at-home test that can help clinicians assess a patient's risk of serious bowel conditions, including bowel cancer, and determine who needs more urgent investigation. This means people at higher risk can be seen sooner, while others can avoid unnecessary invasive procedures and gain reassurance more quickly.

An important point: this pathway is based on symptoms, not age. If someone has bowel symptoms and is referred by their GP, FIT may be recommended regardless of how old they are. This is different to the National Bowel Screening Programme, which is for eligible people (aged 58-74) without symptoms. The National Bowel Screening Programme age of fist eligibility will be lowered down to age 56, from September this year. 

This is another step towards providing the right care, at the right time, for the right people.

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">🌏 World Social Media Day

Every year, Health New Zealand's social media team answers 50,000-80,000 questions, direct messages and comments.

We help people find trusted health information, understand health updates, and connect with the services and support they need. We're a front door to the health system.

Alongside those conversations, we also see abuse between the people in the comment section, and towards our team moderating. The comments in this image are real examples. 

Social media can be a powerful force for connection, learning and support. Every comment, post and share helps shape the kind of online environment we're creating together.

Before you post, comment or share on any social media content, take a moment:
💭 Is it accurate?
💭 Is it helpful?
💭 Would I say this to someone face-to-face?

It's okay to disagree with each other. But remember words have power. There's a real person on the other side of the screen. (And the occasional pesky bot.)

If online experiences are affecting your wellbeing, check the first comment for support and resources.</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">“I came to New Zealand from Saudi Arabia to study medicine on a scholarship, and I’ve built both my professional and personal life here. 

Becoming a doctor was somewhat serendipitous. I didn’t grow up with a lifelong plan to pursue medicine, but when the opportunity arose, I took it. Over time, I discovered how meaningful the profession could be. 

What kept me in medicine was seeing the difference compassionate, evidence-based care can make. 

Medicine combines science, problem-solving and human connection in a way that few careers do. The more patients I met, the more I felt this was where I was meant to be. 

A good day is one where patients receive excellent care, the team works well together, and everyone feels supported. That sense of shared purpose is something I value deeply in medicine. 

It is especially rewarding when I can make a meaningful difference for a patient or family- whether that means helping someone recover from serious illness or taking the time to listen and explain what is happening. 

One of the harder parts is carrying the emotional weight of the job. We meet people on difficult days, and those experiences can stay with you. During intense shifts, I focus on the patient in front of me, take things one step at a time and rely on the team around me. 

Outside work, my family and Muslim faith keep me grounded. Spending time with my daughter helps me recharge and reminds me of what matters most. 

I’m proud of the journey -  coming to New Zealand as a student, completing a PhD, and now training in two specialties. 

I want to be a doctor who combines scientific excellence with genuine compassion. Patients are more than diagnoses and test results. I want them and their families to feel listened to, respected and cared for as people. 

My advice to aspiring doctors is to stay curious, stay humble and never lose sight of the human side of healthcare. None of us becomes a great doctor alone, we learn from our patients, colleagues and mentors every day.” 

- Dr Yassar Alamri, a resident doctor based in Christchurch, undertaking dual training in General Medicine and Intensive Care Medicine. 
</p>

        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">"For me, medicine is deeply connected to family, service and the people who came before me. I’m named after my grandmother in Tonga, who was a district nurse. Our family home was almost like a second hospital; she delivered babies and cared for people throughout her community.

From a young age, my family told me I could stand on her shoulders and take that work one step further. I’ve carried that in my heart ever since.

As a resident doctor, I often describe us as the feet of the medical team. Our senior doctors help set the direction, and we’re there day to day - monitoring patients, carrying plans forward and connecting the wider team.

A good day for me is seeing someone progress. You might first meet a patient seriously unwell and connected to oxygen, then see them walking the corridors a few days later. Being part of that change is amazing.

When work becomes intense, I try to reframe where I am. I remind myself that being a doctor is a privilege, but also that my profession is not all that defines me.

I’m the eldest Tongan daughter. I have responsibilities to my family, church and community, and those parts of my life keep me grounded.

As a Tongan doctor, I know my presence adds to the fabric of healthcare - particularly when a patient sees someone who understands where they come from.

To anyone considering medicine: it's harder than you expect, and it takes support from the people who love you. But the work is needed, you are needed, and it's worthwhile.”

- Dr Emeline Mafi, a resident doctor at Middlemore Hospital.</p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">“When I was growing up, my family used to ask what I wanted to be, and I’d say Mother Teresa. Now I’m in public health, my Mum laughs about it. She says, ‘you used to always say that, and now you’re finally on the right path, helping people’.

I originally trained to be a dentist in India but, to be honest, I’d always dreamed of becoming a doctor. After working in dentistry for six months, I moved to New Zealand and started looking for different opportunities.

That led me to BreastScreen Aotearoa. My job is to encourage wāhine to participate in breast screening and help make the process easier to access and understand.

I work closely with community organisations. I’m a big believer in going to where people are, rather than expecting them to come to us, so you’ll often find me at marae, churches, temples, and local events. If a community needs us, we’ll do our best to be there.

Some of the wāhine I speak with feel nervous about breast screening or have barriers to attending. I listen and help people feel informed and supported enough to make the decision that’s right for them. We work hard to make our services culturally safe and accessible, including offering transport and translation support where needed.

If someone isn’t ready today, that’s okay. My hope is that when they are, they’ll know we’re here for them. 

I often share my own story. Last year I found a lump in my breast and was sent for a mammogram and ultrasound. I remember thinking, ‘oh my god, this is scary’.  I spent weeks worrying and imagining the worst. Thankfully, it turned out to be a non-cancerous cyst. 

The experience gave me a much deeper understanding of the fear and uncertainty many women feel and reminded me how important early detection can be. 

I tell wāhine I was lucky. Your health matters not just for you, but for the people who love and rely on you. A breast screen takes about 20 minutes, with people there who genuinely care. 

I go home feeling grateful for the work that I do. If I’ve helped one woman feel confident enough to take the next step, then it’s been a good day. 

As my Mum likes to remind me, I’ve found the path I was always meant to be on”. 

- Ritu, Health Promotion Recruitment and Retention Advisor
</p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Behind every confident clinician is years of training and experience.

Our Simulation Team at Wellington Regional Hospital design and deliver immersive training that helps teams from all over New Zealand prepare for high-pressure situations before they happen. Using lifelike scenarios, they bring together nurses, doctors and allied health staff to build skills, teamwork and safe decision-making.

The team looks after a specialist simulation centre and its facilities include:

✅ Specialist simulation rooms - recovery, ED and theatre
✅ Presentation and debriefing rooms
✅ Air ambulance simulator (it really 'flies', including with turbulence!)
✅ Skill-based training rooms.
✅ The centre has a range of high-fidelity simulators, part-task trainers and manikins (medical mannequins that can imitate real people including the ability to sweat, bleed, cry and more). 

These smart, capable trainers and their colleagues, behind the scenes, are playing a vital role in helping make care safer for patients across the country.  

These facilities would not be possible without the <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/wellington-hospitals-foundation?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Wellington Hospitals Foundation</a> and its incredibly generous donors, who have played a critical role in helping them come to fruition.
